title.raw: Should You Go to the ER After a Car Accident? Why Feeling Fine Can Fool You
title.rendered: Should You Go to the ER After a Car Accident? Why Feeling Fine Can Fool You

content.raw:
If you have any pain, dizziness, headache, or you hit your head, get checked at an ER the same day as your crash. If you feel completely fine, you are not out of the woods yet. Adrenaline can hide real injuries for hours, and some of the most serious ones show up one to three days later. This guide walks you through the decision: which symptoms mean go now, which delayed signs to watch over the next 72 hours, and when 911 is the only right answer.

Why You Can Feel Fine and Still Be Injured

A crash floods your body with adrenaline and endorphins. Those stress chemicals blunt pain and sharpen focus, which is useful in the moment and misleading afterward. People walk away from wrecks, refuse help at the scene, and wake up the next morning unable to turn their head.

The forces involved do not need to look dramatic. Even a low-speed collision snaps the neck and torso against the seatbelt, and soft-tissue injuries, concussions, and slow internal bleeding all take time to announce themselves. That is why "I feel fine" is a starting point, not a conclusion.

Go to the ER Now: Symptoms That Cannot Wait

Come in the same day if you notice any of the following after a crash:

  • Chest pain or shortness of breath. The seatbelt saves lives, but bruised ribs and cardiac strain need a real workup. Our chest pain evaluation runs an EKG and imaging within minutes.
  • A headache that builds, or any head strike. A blow to the head deserves evaluation before you sleep it off.
  • Abdominal pain, swelling, or a seatbelt bruise. A band of bruising across the belly can signal internal injury.
  • Numbness, tingling, or weakness in an arm or leg.
  • Confusion, unusual drowsiness, or vision changes.
  • New neck or back pain that worsens with movement.

Call 911 instead of driving if there is uncontrolled bleeding, a suspected spine injury, loss of consciousness, or someone who cannot safely move.

Delayed Symptoms: What to Watch for 72 Hours

Some crash injuries follow their own clock. Watch for these over the next three days:

  • Neck stiffness and pain. Whiplash symptoms often appear a day or more after the crash, according to MedlinePlus.
  • Headache, fogginess, or mood and sleep changes. MedlinePlus notes concussion symptoms can be subtle and delayed. Our concussion treatment page covers the warning signs in depth.
  • Growing abdominal pain, swelling, or deep bruising. Slow internal bleeding can take hours to days to show.
  • Tingling that spreads, which can point to a nerve or disc injury.

Anyone on blood thinners, anyone pregnant, and any child involved in a crash should be evaluated the same day even without symptoms. The risk calculation is different for these groups.

What the ER Checks After a Crash

A post-accident visit is a systematic search for what adrenaline is hiding. A physician examines your head, neck, spine, chest, and abdomen, then orders the right studies from our on-site imaging suite: CT for the head and internal organs, X-ray for bones, ultrasound for soft tissue and bleeding.

Every finding is documented. That record matters for your recovery plan, and it matters for any insurance claim, because it ties your injuries to the crash with a timestamp. If someone else caused the accident, ask our team about a letter of protection, which lets treatment start while a claim is pending.

High-speed wrecks bring their own injury patterns. We cover those separately in our guide to high-speed car accident injuries.

911, ER, or Watch at Home?

  • Call 911: uncontrolled bleeding, unconsciousness, suspected spine injury, severe chest pain, or anyone trapped or unable to move safely.
  • Go to the ER today: any symptom from the lists above, any head strike, a crash at highway speed, or a passenger who is pregnant, a child, or on blood thinners.
  • Watch at home: a genuinely minor bump with zero symptoms, in a healthy adult, with someone available to watch for changes. Recheck yourself at 24, 48, and 72 hours, and come in the moment anything develops.

Get Checked Today, Not Next Week

The trauma and car accident team at ER of Irving evaluates crash injuries around the clock, with CT, X-ray, ultrasound, and lab work under one roof. Walk in any hour at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX, or call (972) 893-3148. For life-threatening injuries, call 911 first.

FAQs

How long after a car accident can injuries show up?

Most delayed injuries surface within 24 to 72 hours, which is why that window matters for self-checks. Whiplash can take a day or longer to stiffen, concussion symptoms can drift in over several days, and slow internal bleeding may build for hours before pain appears.

Should I get checked after a minor fender bender?

Get checked if you have any symptom at all, hit your head, are pregnant, take blood thinners, or a child was in the car. A truly symptom-free healthy adult can watch at home for 72 hours, but the threshold for coming in should stay low.

Do I need an appointment for a post-accident checkup?

No. ER of Irving is walk-in only, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. An experienced emergency physician examines you, orders imaging on the spot when it is needed, and reviews the results with you during the same visit.

Why does the ER visit matter for my insurance claim?

Because it creates a timestamped medical record connecting your injuries to the crash. Waiting a week weakens both your recovery and your documentation. If another driver caused the accident, ask about a letter of protection so treatment does not wait on the claim.

title.raw: How Long Does Food Poisoning Last? Recovery Timeline and Warning Signs
title.rendered: How Long Does Food Poisoning Last? Recovery Timeline and Warning Signs

content.raw:
You ate something a few hours ago, and now your stomach is in knots. The first question most people ask is simple: how long will this last? For most healthy adults, food poisoning clears up on its own in about one to three days. But the timeline depends on which germ made you sick, and a few symptoms mean you should stop waiting it out and get medical care. Here is what to expect, and how to tell an ordinary bad night from an emergency.

How Long Does Food Poisoning Usually Last?

Most cases of food poisoning are short. Symptoms come on fast, feel awful for a day or two, then fade as your body clears the germ. According to MedlinePlus, most people with foodborne illness get better on their own without treatment. The catch is that "food poisoning" is not one illness. It is a group of illnesses caused by different bacteria and viruses, and each one has its own timeline. That is why your sister can feel fine six hours after the same meal that had you up all night.

Timeline by Cause: Onset and Duration

The FoodSafety.gov and CDC data show how much the timing varies by germ. This table gives a rough guide for the most common causes: These are typical ranges, not promises. Your age, general health, and how much of the germ you swallowed all change the picture.

Why the Food You Blame Is Often the Wrong One

People tend to blame the last thing they ate. But because onset times run so long for some germs, the meal that made you sick could be from two or three days ago. A slow-starting illness like Campylobacter points back to something you ate days before symptoms began, not last night's dinner. This is why tracking the exact food is hard, and why the cause often stays a mystery even after you recover.

When Food Poisoning Becomes an Emergency

Most cases are miserable but safe to ride out at home. Some are not. The CDC lists five signs of severe food poisoning that mean you should get medical care. Do not wait these out:
  • Bloody diarrhea
  • Diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days
  • A fever over 102°F
  • Vomiting so often you cannot keep any liquids down
  • Signs of dehydration, such as little or no urination, a very dry mouth and throat, or feeling dizzy when you stand up
Any single one of these is a good reason to get checked. Dehydration is the most common way food poisoning turns dangerous, because losing fluids faster than you can replace them strains the whole body. Our guide on recognizing the signs of dehydration covers what to watch for in more detail.

Who Needs to Be More Careful

Some people get sicker from the same germ and dehydrate faster. The CDC flags these groups as higher risk:
  • Children under 5
  • Adults 65 and older
  • People who are pregnant
  • People with weakened immune systems or chronic illness
If you are caring for a baby or young child who cannot keep liquids down, do not wait for the symptom list above. Children dehydrate quickly, and our guide on pediatric dehydration explains the early warning signs a parent should never ignore.

How to Recover at Home

For a routine case with none of the warning signs above, home care is usually enough. The goal is to stay hydrated while your body does the work:
  • Sip small amounts of clear fluids often, rather than gulping a lot at once.
  • Ease back into bland foods like toast, rice, or bananas when your stomach settles.
  • Rest, and skip alcohol and caffeine until you feel better.
  • Avoid anti-diarrhea medicine if you have a high fever or bloody stools, since it can make some infections worse.
If you are keeping fluids down and slowly improving each day, that is the normal path. If you are losing ground instead, it is time to get help.

How ER of Irving Treats Food Poisoning

When food poisoning crosses into an emergency, the fastest fix for dehydration is fluids given directly into a vein. At ER of Irving, our team can start IV fluids within minutes, run lab tests to find the cause, and check for complications, all on site and open 24/7. You can learn more on our food poisoning treatment page. If your symptoms match any of the CDC warning signs, walk in any hour or call (972) 893-3148.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does food poisoning last in adults?

Most healthy adults recover in about 1 to 3 days, though some germs like Salmonella and Campylobacter can cause symptoms that last a week or more.

How fast does food poisoning start after eating?

It depends on the germ. Staph can hit within 4 to 10 hours, while others like Campylobacter may take 2 to 5 days. Because of this range, the food you blame is often not the one that made you sick.

When should I go to the ER for food poisoning?

Get emergency care if you have bloody diarrhea, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, a fever over 102°F, vomiting that keeps you from holding down liquids, or signs of dehydration like little urination and dizziness.

Is it food poisoning or a stomach bug?

The symptoms overlap and can be hard to tell apart. A stomach bug (viral gastroenteritis) usually spreads person to person, while food poisoning comes from contaminated food or drink. Either way, the warning signs for when to seek care are the same.

What is the fastest way to recover from food poisoning?

There is no cure that speeds up clearing the germ, so the focus is staying hydrated and resting. Sip clear fluids often, ease back into bland foods, and get medical care if you cannot keep liquids down.

title.raw: Hantavirus: What Irving Residents Need to Know to Stay Safe
title.rendered: Hantavirus: What Irving Residents Need to Know to Stay Safe

content.raw:
If you are a North Texas resident, you likely value the peace of your suburban home, the efficiency of your local storage units, and the comfort of your garage or shed. However, as the weather shifts or as we engage in seasonal cleaning, we often come into contact with uninvited guests: rodents. While most of us view mice as a mere nuisance, they can carry a silent and potentially deadly threat known as Hantavirus. Hantavirus is rare; many people and even some healthcare providers may not recognize it until it becomes a critical emergency. This guide is designed to help you understand the risks, identify Hantavirus symptoms, and know exactly when to seek life-saving care

What is Hantavirus and How is it Spread in North Texas?

According to the CDC, hantavirus is a family of viruses spread primarily by rodents. In the United States, the most common form is Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease that can be fatal if not treated urgently. Unlike the common cold, which spreads through human coughing or sneezing, Hantavirus is a "zoonotic" disease, meaning it jumps from animals to humans.

Common Rodent Carriers in the Irving Area

While many rodents live in North Texas, not all carry Hantavirus. According to the NPS, the primary culprit in North America is the Deer Mouse. These mice are easily identified by their white bellies and large ears. Other local carriers include the Cotton Rat and the White-footed Mouse. It is important to remember that you cannot tell if a mouse is carrying the virus just by looking at it. An infected rodent appears perfectly healthy while shedding the virus in its urine, droppings, and saliva.

Understanding "Aerosolization": How Humans Get Sick

The most common way people contract the virus is through a process called aerosolization. When rodent urine or droppings are disturbed, such as when you sweep out a dusty garage or move boxes in an attic, tiny droplets containing the virus are kicked up into the air. When you breathe in this contaminated "mist," the virus enters your lungs.

Recognizing the Signs: Hantavirus Symptoms vs. The Common Flu

The greatest challenge with Hantavirus is that it begins quietly. Because the initial Hantavirus symptoms feel exactly like a standard viral infection, many patients stay home, assuming they just have a "bad flu."

Early Warning Signs (The Prodromal Phase)

For the first 1 to 8 weeks after exposure, the virus incubates in your body. Once the "prodromal" phase begins, you may experience:
  • Fever and Chills: A sudden high temperature is often the first sign.
  • Muscle Aches: Significant pain in the large muscle groups, such as the thighs, hips, and back.
  • Fatigue: An overwhelming sense of tiredness that doesn't improve with rest.
  • Gastrointestinal Distress: About half of HPS patients experience nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, which can lead to misdiagnosis as a "stomach bug."

The Critical Turning Point: When to Seek Emergency Care

About 4 to 10 days after the initial Hantavirus symptoms begin, the disease moves into its most dangerous stage. This is the Emergency Phase, where the virus begins to leak fluid into the lungs (pulmonary edema). Seek immediate emergency care at the ER if you experience:
  1. Shortness of Breath: Feeling like you cannot get enough air, even while resting.
  2. Coughing: A persistent, dry cough that worsens quickly.
  3. Chest Tightness: A feeling of heavy pressure on your chest.
  4. Rapid Heart Rate: A heart that feels like it is racing or fluttering.
CDC guidelines emphasize that if you have a history of rodent exposure and develop these symptoms, you must tell your healthcare provider immediately.

2026 Health Update: The Global Andes Virus Outbreak

As of May 2026, the global health community is monitoring a specific strain of Hantavirus known as the Andes virus. While most hantaviruses do not spread from person to person, the Andes virus is a notable exception. The CDC recently issued a Health Alert regarding a cluster of Andes virus cases linked to a cruise ship in the Atlantic. While this outbreak is currently contained to specific travelers, it highlights the importance of being aware of "atypical" symptoms. Unlike the strains common in Texas, the Andes virus can be transmitted through prolonged close contact with an infected person's respiratory secretions. If you have recently traveled internationally or have been in close contact with someone who has, please share this information with our triage team upon arrival.

Preventing Hantavirus in Your Irving Home and Property

Prevention is your first line of defense. By making your home less attractive to rodents, you significantly decrease your risk of exposure.

Rodent-Proofing Your Garage, Attic, and Shed

  • Seal Entry Points: Mice can fit through a hole the size of a pencil eraser. Use steel wool and caulk to seal gaps around pipes, doors, and vents.
  • Proper Food Storage: Keep pet food and pantry items in thick plastic or metal containers with tight-fitting lids.
  • Clean Up the Yard: Remove woodpiles, tall grass, and clutter from the perimeter of your home where rodents like to nest.

Safe Cleanup: Why You Should Never Sweep Droppings

If you find rodent droppings in your home, do not reach for a broom or vacuum. Sweeping pushes the virus into the air, where you are most likely to inhale it. According to CDC cleaning protocols, you should:
  1. Ventilate: Open doors and windows for at least 30 minutes before cleaning.
  2. Wet it Down: Spray the area with a disinfectant or a mixture of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water. Let it soak for 5 minutes.
  3. Wipe, Don't Sweep: Use paper towels to pick up the waste while wearing rubber or plastic gloves.
  4. Dispose: Seal everything in a plastic bag and place it in a covered trash can.

Don’t Wait, Your Health is Our Priority

If you develop shortness of breath, chest tightness, or a high fever after contact with rodents or their droppings, do not wait. Tell the triage team about the exposure and get emergency care for breathing problems at ER of Irving right away. We are open 24/7. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional. Stay informed with helpful tips on recognizing respiratory symptoms and keeping your family safe. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

Can my dog or cat catch Hantavirus and give it to me?

No, domestic pets like cats and dogs are not known to transmit Hantavirus to humans. However, they may bring infected rodents into the house, so it is important to maintain flea and rodent control for your pets.

How long does the virus live in the environment?

The virus is relatively fragile. It generally loses its ability to infect people within 2 to 3 days when exposed to normal sunlight and household temperatures. However, in dark, cool areas like a crawl space, it may persist longer.

Is there a vaccine for Hantavirus? 

Currently, there is no FDA-approved vaccine for Hantavirus in the United States. Prevention and early medical intervention are the most effective ways to stay safe.

Can I get Hantavirus from a mouse bite?

Yes, though it is much less common than breathing in contaminated dust, bites from an infected rodent can transmit the virus.

content.raw:
The energy of the 2026 World Cup is finally here, and Dallas-Fort Worth is at the center of the action. Whether you are cheering in the stands, tailgating outside the stadium, or attending a crowded fan fest, the atmosphere is electric. However, for those visiting from cooler climates, there is an opponent more formidable than any striker on the pitch: the Texas summer. In North Texas, June and July temperatures frequently soar above 100°F (38°C), often accompanied by high humidity that makes it difficult for the body to cool itself. We want you to enjoy every minute of this historic tournament, which is why understanding the risks of heat-related illness is vital. 

Welcome to Texas: Preparing for the Summer Heat at the 2026 World Cup

Texas is famous for its hospitality, but its summer weather can be unforgiving. For World Cup fans, the risk isn't just the temperature; it’s the "heat index," which measures how hot it feels when relative humidity is factored in. According to the National Weather Service, high humidity levels can hinder the evaporation of sweat, your body’s primary way of cooling down. When thousands of fellow fans surround you in a stadium or an outdoor watch party, the ambient temperature can rise even higher. Being prepared means more than just wearing your team’s jersey; it means having a hydration plan and knowing when your body is signaling for help.

Understanding Heat-Related Illnesses: Heat Exhaustion vs. Heat Stroke

Heat-related illnesses exist on a spectrum. They often start with mild heat cramps and progress to heat exhaustion. If left untreated, heat exhaustion can quickly escalate into heat stroke, which is a life-threatening emergency.

Warning Signs of Heat Exhaustion

Heat exhaustion occurs when your body loses excessive amounts of water and salt, typically through heavy sweating. Fans tailgating in the parking lots for hours are particularly susceptible. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identifies these common symptoms of heat exhaustion:
  • Heavy sweating and cold, pale, clammy skin.
  • A fast, weak pulse.
  • Nausea or vomiting.
  • Muscle cramps.
  • Tiredness or weakness.
  • Dizziness and fainting.
If you or a friend feels these symptoms, it is time to take immediate action. Move to an air-conditioned space, loosen your clothing, and sip water. If symptoms last longer than one hour or worsen, you should head to a nearby clinic or an emergency room for heat stroke evaluation to ensure the condition isn't progressing.

Recognizing Heat Stroke (A True Medical Emergency)

Heat stroke is the most serious heat-related illness. It occurs when the body’s core temperature rises to 104°F (40°C) or higher within minutes. At this point, the body’s cooling system fails, and the internal organs are at risk of permanent damage. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), you must call 911 or seek an emergency room for heat stroke immediately if you notice:
  • High body temperature (103°F or higher).
  • Hot, red, dry, or damp skin (note that in heat stroke, the person may stop sweating).
  • Fast, strong pulse.
  • Confusion, agitation, or slurred speech.
  • Loss of consciousness (passing out).
Pro-Tip for Fans: If you see a fellow fan who appears confused or has stopped sweating despite the heat, do not wait. This is a medical emergency. Move them to a cooler place and seek professional help immediately.

Don’t Let Dehydration Ruin the Match: Spotting the Signs Early

Dehydration happens when you use or lose more fluid than you take in. Between the excitement of the game and the consumption of salty stadium snacks or alcoholic beverages, it is very easy to fall behind on your fluid intake.

Common Signs of Dehydration for Adult Fans

While thirst is an obvious sign, it is often a "late" indicator; by the time you feel thirsty, you may already be dehydrated. MedlinePlus suggests looking for these earlier warning signs:
  • Extreme thirst and a very dry mouth.
  • Dark-colored urine (it should ideally be the color of light lemonade).
  • Decreased urination.
  • Fatigue or "brain fog."
  • Dizziness or lightheadedness.
To stay ahead, try the "one-for-one" rule: for every alcoholic or caffeinated beverage you enjoy, drink at least 8 to 12 ounces of water.

Traveling with Kids? Watch for Pediatric Dehydration

If you are bringing young fans to the 2026 World Cup, please be extra vigilant. Children’s bodies heat up three to five times faster than adults'. Watch for these signs in children:
  • Dry tongue and lips.
  • No tears when crying.
  • Sunken eyes or cheeks.
  • Listlessness or irritability.
  • Fewer than six wet diapers (for infants) or no urination for several hours in older children.
If a child is unable to keep liquids down or seems unusually sleepy, they may need medical intervention. Visiting an emergency room for heat stroke or severe dehydration can provide the rapid care they need to recover.

Proactive Cooling: Tips for the Stadium and Fan Zone

Prevention is the best strategy for enjoying the World Cup safely. Follow these simple steps to protect yourself and your family:
  1. Wear Light Clothing: Choose loose-fitting, light-colored garments made of moisture-wicking fabric.
  2. Schedule Your Sun: If possible, spend the hottest part of the day (11:00 AM to 4:00 PM) in air-conditioned fan zones or indoor venues.
  3. Use Electrolytes: Pure water is great, but if you are sweating excessively, you also need to replace salt and minerals. MedlinePlus states that Sports drinks or electrolyte powders can help maintain your electrolyte balance.
  4. Sunscreen is Vital: A sunburn affects your body’s ability to cool itself. Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30 as recommended by the FDA.

Fast Relief at the ER of Irving: When to Seek Medical Help

Sometimes, despite our best efforts, the Texas sun wins. When shade and water aren't enough to bring relief, medical intervention becomes necessary.

Getting IV Fluids for Severe Dehydration

When you are severely dehydrated, your stomach may struggle to absorb water fast enough, or nausea might prevent you from drinking at all. In these cases, IV Fluid Therapy is the gold standard of care. By delivering fluids and essential electrolytes directly into the bloodstream, we can bypass the digestive system for immediate rehydration. This helps stabilize your blood pressure, restores organ function, and alleviates the crushing fatigue and headache associated with heat illness. If you find yourself unable to recover after an hour in the shade, visiting an emergency room for heat stroke symptoms or severe dehydration is the safest choice.

24/7 No-Wait Emergency Care Near the Action

We know you didn't travel across the world to sit in a waiting room. ER of Irving provides emergency care for heat-related illness 24 hours a day. For heat-related illness, treatment may include active cooling and IV fluids to restore hydration and electrolytes. If you are visiting for the World Cup or live in the area, ER of Irving treats heat stroke and severe dehydration around the clock.

Don’t Let the Heat Keep You on the Sidelines

If you or a loved one is struggling with the intense Texas sun, don't wait for the condition to become life-threatening. Your health is the priority, so you can get back to the game you love. If cooling and water are not enough, or you see signs of heat stroke such as confusion, no sweating, or a very high temperature, call 911 or seek emergency care right away. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

How do I know if I should go to the emergency room for heat stroke?

If your temperature is over 100°F, you feel confused, or you have stopped sweating, you must seek an emergency room for heat stroke immediately. These are signs that your body can no longer regulate its own temperature.

Is it safe to drink just water in the Texas heat?

While water is essential, if you are sweating a lot, you also lose electrolytes like sodium and potassium. It is often better to mix in a sports drink or an electrolyte solution to prevent an imbalance.

Can I get heat stroke even if it’s cloudy?

Yes. High humidity can be just as dangerous as direct sunlight because it prevents sweat from evaporating, which is how your body cools down. Always check the "heat index" rather than just the temperature.

What is the fastest way to recover from heat exhaustion?

Move to a cool area, lie down with your feet slightly elevated, and use cool compresses on your neck and armpits. If you don't feel better within 30-60 minutes, you may need professional medical care and IV fluids.

How much water should I drink during a World Cup match?

A general rule of thumb is to drink about 8 ounces of water every 20 minutes while in the heat. Don't wait until you are thirsty to start drinking.

Are children more at risk for dehydration than adults?

Yes. Children have a higher surface-area-to-mass ratio and produce more metabolic heat per unit of body mass, making them much more vulnerable to the heat.

content.raw:
Some symptoms can wait until morning. Many cannot. Knowing the difference between "watch and wait" and "go now" is what saves brain tissue, heart muscle, and lives. This guide covers 8 emergencies that need 24-hour ER care, the warning signs to watch for, and why ER of Irving is set up to handle them around the clock.

1. Stroke Symptoms (Face, Arm, Speech, Time)

A stroke kills around 1.9 million brain cells every minute it goes untreated. The CDC teaches the F.A.S.T. method to recognize one fast.
  • F – Face drooping on one side
  • A – Arm weakness when raising both arms
  • S – Speech difficulty or slurred words
  • T – Time to call 911 immediately
Even if symptoms fade, get evaluated. A transient ischemic attack (mini-stroke) raises the risk of a full stroke within hours or days. See our full F.A.S.T. stroke guide for details.

2. Heart Attack Signs

Heart attacks rarely match what people see on TV. Most feel like pressure, not stabbing pain. Call 911 if you have:
  • Chest pressure or squeezing lasting more than a few minutes
  • Pain spreading to the jaw, arm, neck, or back
  • Shortness of breath with the chest pain
  • Cold sweats, nausea, or lightheadedness
Women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical signs like fatigue or jaw pain without classic chest pressure. Do not drive yourself. An ambulance starts care en route.

3. Severe Allergic Reaction (Anaphylaxis)

Anaphylaxis can close your airway within minutes. Use an EpiPen if you have one, then go to the ER. Even after EpiPen use, a second wave can occur 4 to 12 hours later. Warning signs:
  • Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue
  • Hives spreading across the body
  • Difficulty breathing or wheezing
  • Sudden severe drop in blood pressure (fainting)
  • Severe vomiting or diarrhea
See our anaphylaxis after EpiPen guide for what happens after the first dose.

4. High Fever in Babies and Young Children

Fever in young children is different from fever in adults. The age and behavior change matter more than the number. Go to the ER if your child has:
  • Any rectal fever in a baby under 3 months
  • Fever over 102°F in a child 3 to 6 months
  • Fever lasting more than 5 days
  • Fever with stiff neck, severe headache, or rash
  • Fever with extreme drowsiness or trouble waking
The MedlinePlus guide on fever covers age-specific thresholds in detail. Our 103° fever rule for children covers when to head in immediately.

5. Severe Abdominal Pain

Most belly pain is not an emergency. Some types are. Head to the ER for:
  • Sharp pain in the lower right belly (possible appendicitis)
  • Pain so severe you cannot stand straight or walk
  • Pain with vomiting blood or bloody stools
  • Pain with fever and a hard, rigid belly
  • Sudden severe pain in pregnancy
Our abdominal pain service page covers the ER workup.

6. Sudden Severe Headache

A "thunderclap" headache, peaking in seconds, can signal a bleed in or around the brain. This is one of the highest-priority symptoms in an ER. Red flags:
  • Worst headache of your life, starting suddenly
  • Headache with stiff neck or fever
  • Headache after a head injury
  • Headache with vision changes or one-sided weakness
  • Headache with confusion or trouble speaking
See our migraine vs aneurysm guide for how to tell them apart.

7. Difficulty Breathing

Breathing problems can come from asthma, pneumonia, heart failure, blood clots, or allergic reactions. The cause matters less than acting fast. Call 911 if:
  • You cannot speak in full sentences
  • Lips or fingertips turn blue
  • Sudden severe shortness of breath at rest
  • Wheezing not responding to inhalers
Our emergency breathing care page details the ER pathway.

8. Deep Cuts and Broken Bones

Some injuries need same-day repair. Stitches are most effective within the first 6 to 8 hours. ER-level injuries:
  • Cuts that gape open or will not stop bleeding after 10 minutes of pressure
  • Cuts on the face, hands, or joints
  • Visible bone, tendon, or deep fat
  • Broken bones with deformity or skin breakage
  • Loss of feeling or movement past the injury
Our fractures treatment page covers imaging and stabilization.

Why a 24-Hour ER (Not Calling 911 Tomorrow)

ER of Irving is a freestanding emergency facility licensed under Texas Health & Safety Code Chapter 254A. We operate around the clock with experienced ER physicians, on-site imaging, and full lab services.
  • CT scan, x-ray, ultrasound, and labs available 24/7
  • Experienced ER physicians on-site every hour of the day
  • Walk-in with no appointment needed
  • Transfer arrangements with regional hospitals for ICU or surgery cases
For symptoms above, do not wait until morning. The cost of waiting is measured in brain cells, heart muscle, or surgical urgency. The cost of an unneeded ER visit is much smaller. Not sure your symptom needs an ER at all? Our emergency room vs 24-hour pharmacy guide covers what a pharmacist can and cannot handle.

Call Now Get Direction

FAQs

Is ER of Irving open 24 hours?

Yes. Our freestanding emergency room is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, every day of the year. No appointment is needed.

When should I call 911 vs drive to the ER?

Call 911 for stroke, heart attack, severe trouble breathing, anaphylaxis, or any situation where moving the patient could make things worse. Driving is fine for stable cuts, fractures, or moderate pain.

What is a freestanding ER?

A freestanding emergency room provides full emergency care with experienced ER physicians, on-site imaging, and labs, but without inpatient beds. If you need admission or surgery, we transfer you to a partner hospital. Our guide on how a standalone ER works for busy Irving families explains the visit flow step by step.

Is a freestanding ER the same as urgent care?

No. Urgent care handles minor conditions (mild infections, simple cuts). A freestanding ER handles life-threatening emergencies. Billing and licensing are different. Our ER vs urgent care guide breaks down which to choose for common situations.

Do I need insurance to visit the ER?

Federal law (EMTALA) requires every ER to evaluate and stabilize you regardless of insurance or ability to pay. Bring an ID and insurance card if you have them, but do not delay care to find them.

title.rendered: Chest Pain: Muscular, Lung, or Heart? Key Differences

content.raw:
Chest pain is one of the scariest symptoms a person can feel. The fear of a heart attack is real, but most chest pain is not cardiac. It can also come from muscles, the lungs, or anxiety. This guide covers how to tell muscular, lung, and heart chest pain apart, the red flags that mean you should not wait, and how the ER tells them apart fast.

Why Chest Pain Is Hard to Diagnose at Home

The chest holds the heart, lungs, esophagus, ribs, and many large muscles. All of them can produce sharp or aching pain that radiates and confuses you. According to MedlinePlus, chest pain has dozens of possible causes ranging from muscle strain to life-threatening events. Self-diagnosis is unreliable because symptoms overlap heavily. Knowing the patterns helps you decide between waiting it out and calling 911.

Muscular Chest Pain: How It Feels

Muscular chest pain is the most common cause of non-cardiac chest pain. It usually comes from a pulled chest muscle, costochondritis, or rib strain.

Common signs:

  • Sharp pain that worsens with movement. Twisting, reaching, or deep breathing makes it worse.
  • Tenderness when pressed. Pressing on the spot reproduces the pain.
  • Pain stays in one area. It does not spread to the jaw, arm, or back.
  • No other symptoms. No sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath.
For another muscular cause that mimics heart pain, see our slipping rib syndrome guide.

Lung-Related Chest Pain: Pleurisy, Pneumonia, and PE

Pain from the lungs or the lining around them feels different from muscle pain. The breathing connection is the giveaway.

Common signs:

  • Pain that worsens with deep breaths. Each inhale produces a sharp catch.
  • Cough, fever, or colored mucus. Suggests pneumonia or bronchitis.
  • Sudden shortness of breath. Especially after a long flight, surgery, or sitting still for hours.
  • Coughing up blood. Always an ER visit.
MedlinePlus notes that a pulmonary embolism (blood clot in the lung) often presents as sudden chest pain with shortness of breath and can be fatal if untreated. PE is one of the most missed emergencies because the chest pain feels musculoskeletal at first.

Heart-Related Chest Pain: Heart Attack, Angina, Pericarditis

Cardiac chest pain often does not feel "sharp." It feels like pressure, squeezing, or a heavy weight.

Common signs:

  • Pressure or crushing sensation in the center of the chest.
  • Pain that spreads to the jaw, neck, arm (often left), or back.
  • Other body symptoms. Cold sweats, nausea, lightheadedness, shortness of breath.
  • Pain that lasts more than a few minutes or returns repeatedly.
  • Pain not affected by movement or breathing. Sitting still does not change it.
The CDC reports that women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical heart attack symptoms: jaw pain, fatigue, or nausea without the classic chest pressure.

4 Key Differences That Help You Decide

Question Muscular Lung Heart
Worse with deep breaths? Sometimes Yes, strongly No
Worse with movement? Yes Sometimes No
Tender to press? Yes No No
Sweating, nausea, jaw pain? No Sometimes Often
If your answers point to lung or heart, get evaluated. Muscular pain is the only group where home care is safe to try first.

Red Flags That Need Emergency Care

Call 911 or go to the nearest ER if you have any of these:
  • Pressure or squeezing in the center of the chest lasting more than a few minutes
  • Pain spreading to the jaw, arm, or back
  • Shortness of breath with chest pain
  • Sudden severe chest pain with sweating, nausea, or fainting
  • Coughing up blood
  • Severe pain after long travel or recent surgery (PE risk)
Do not drive yourself if cardiac symptoms are present. An ambulance starts care en route and alerts the ER team.

How ER of Irving Tells Them Apart

At ER of Irving, the chest pain pathway uses imaging and labs to rule the dangerous causes in or out fast:
  • EKG within minutes of arrival to check for cardiac changes
  • Troponin blood test to look for heart muscle damage
  • Chest x-ray for pneumonia, collapsed lung, or fluid
  • CT scan if pulmonary embolism is suspected
  • Physical exam for tenderness, breath sounds, and muscle involvement
Most patients get a clear answer within 60 to 90 minutes.

Call Now Get Direction

FAQs

How long does muscular chest pain last?

Most muscular chest pain improves within 1 to 2 weeks with rest, ice, and over-the-counter pain relief. Persistent pain beyond 3 weeks should be checked.

Can lung problems feel like a heart attack?

Yes. A pulmonary embolism can mimic a heart attack with chest pain and shortness of breath. The ER uses CT imaging and blood tests to tell them apart.

What is costochondritis?

Inflammation of the cartilage that connects ribs to the breastbone. It causes sharp chest pain that worsens with movement and is tender to touch.

Can anxiety cause real chest pain?

Yes. Panic attacks produce chest tightness, racing heart, and shortness of breath that mimic a heart attack. The ER can rule out cardiac causes safely.

Is chest pain on the left side always the heart?

No. The heart sits more centrally than people think. Left-sided chest pain can be muscular, lung, or stomach acid. The ER tests for cardiac causes regardless.

title.raw: Hairline Fracture Symptoms: 7 Signs You Need an ER X-Ray
title.rendered: Hairline Fracture Symptoms: 7 Signs You Need an ER X-Ray

content.raw:
A hairline fracture is one of the trickiest injuries to spot. The bone has a thin crack but stays mostly intact, so swelling and bruising can be mild. Many people walk on a broken foot for days, thinking it is a sprain. This guide covers 7 symptoms that point to a hairline fracture, why some x-rays miss them, and when to head to the ER for imaging.

What is a Hairline Fracture?

A hairline fracture is a small crack in a bone, usually caused by repetitive force or a single hard impact. The bone surface looks intact, but the crack runs through one or more layers. According to MedlinePlus, hairline fractures fall under the broader category of stress fractures and account for a meaningful share of overuse injuries in athletes and active adults. These fractures are most common in weight-bearing bones. Feet, shins, and hips see the highest rates, but they can happen anywhere.

7 Symptoms of a Hairline Fracture

Some of these signs mimic a sprain or pulled muscle. The pattern of how they show up is what matters.

1. Localized Pain at One Specific Spot

The pain stays in one area you can point to with one finger. Sprains and bruises usually spread across a wider zone. A hairline fracture feels sharp at the crack itself.

2. Pain That Worsens With Activity

You feel fine resting, but the moment you walk, run, or load the bone, pain returns. The pain pattern is dose-dependent: more activity, more pain.

3. Swelling Without Heavy Bruising

A torn muscle or ligament usually bruises within 24 hours. Hairline fractures often swell without much color change. The skin may look only mildly puffy. If bruising is your main symptom, our guide to telling a bone bruise from a fracture covers how the two differ.

4. Tenderness When You Press the Bone

If pressing directly on a small area of bone causes sharp pain, that is a strong fracture signal. The technical term is "point tenderness."

5. Pain That Does Not Resolve With Rest

A pulled muscle or mild sprain usually feels better within 3 to 5 days of rest. Hairline fractures take longer and often hurt at rest after the first week.

6. Limited Weight-Bearing or Grip Strength

Foot or shin fractures make people limp or shift weight. Hand and wrist fractures reduce grip strength, especially with rotation movements.

7. Pain That Feels Worse at Night

A common but underrecognized sign. NIH research on stress fractures notes increased pain at rest as the injury progresses, often peaking when you lie down.

Common Causes of Hairline Fractures

Most hairline fractures fall into two camps:
  • Repetitive overuse. Running long distances, marching, jumping, or training without rest days. The bone fatigues faster than it heals.
  • Single hard impact. A fall onto an outstretched hand, a stubbed toe with bone-on-floor contact, or a sports collision.
Older adults with osteoporosis can develop hairline fractures from low-impact events like rolling over in bed or stepping off a curb.

Where Hairline Fractures Happen Most Often

The bones that take the most weight see the most of these injuries.
  • Tibia (shin). The top site, especially in runners.
  • Metatarsals (foot bones). Common in dancers, walkers, and people who increased activity quickly.
  • Navicular (mid-foot). Hard to diagnose; missed on standard x-rays often.
  • Hip (femoral neck). Serious if missed; can become a full fracture.
  • Pelvis, calcaneus (heel), and ribs. Less common but real.

Why X-Rays Sometimes Miss Hairline Fractures

A hairline fracture can be invisible on the first x-ray. The crack is too fine to show clearly, especially in the first 7 to 14 days. The bone needs time to start healing for the fracture line to become visible. Doctors call this a callus forming around the crack. If your initial x-ray is negative but symptoms persist, the ER may order:
  • Repeat x-ray in 10 to 14 days, when the callus shows up
  • CT scan for higher-resolution imaging
  • MRI when soft tissue and bone marrow signal is needed
Telling your provider exactly how the pain behaves matters more than the first x-ray result.

When to Visit the ER vs Wait

Some hairline fractures need immediate evaluation. Others can wait for a primary care visit. Go to the ER of Irving right away if:
  • You cannot bear weight at all
  • Pain is sharp and constant, even at rest
  • The area is severely swollen or deformed
  • You suspect a hip, pelvis, or skull fracture
  • Numbness, tingling, or color change in the limb
Same-day imaging and pain control happen faster at an ER than waiting for a clinic appointment. For suspected hip fractures in particular, delays can become surgical emergencies.

How ER of Irving Diagnoses Hairline Fractures

The ER evaluation usually follows this path:
  • Exam. Point tenderness, range of motion, and weight-bearing tests
  • Imaging. X-ray first, then CT or MRI if the x-ray is negative but suspicion stays high
  • Stabilization. Splint, cast, or boot to immobilize the bone
  • Pain management. Anti-inflammatories and short-term analgesics
  • Follow-up plan. Orthopedic referral when needed

FAQs

How long does a hairline fracture take to heal?

Most hairline fractures heal in 6 to 8 weeks with rest and immobilization. Hip and navicular fractures can take 12 weeks or more.

Can you walk on a hairline fracture?

You often can, but you should not. Walking on it delays healing and can turn a hairline crack into a full fracture. A boot or crutches keep weight off the bone.

What is the difference between a hairline fracture and a stress fracture?

The terms overlap. A stress fracture is caused by repetitive force; a hairline fracture is the type of crack. Most stress fractures appear as hairline fractures on imaging.

Will a hairline fracture show on the first x-ray?

Not always. The crack can take 1 to 2 weeks to become visible as the bone starts to heal. A repeat x-ray or MRI is often needed.

Do I need a cast for a hairline fracture?

Many heal in a boot or splint without a hard cast. The bone needs immobilization, but full casting is reserved for unstable fractures or specific sites.

title.raw: Poison Ivy and Oak: When the Rash Requires the ER
title.rendered: Poison Ivy and Oak: When the Rash Requires the ER

content.raw:
It starts as a faint pink streak or a small cluster of itchy bumps. You might recall brushing against some brush while gardening or hiking over the weekend. For most people, a run-in with poison ivy, oak, or sumac is a rite of passage, a miserable week of itching followed by a slow recovery. However, for some, what starts as a minor irritation can quickly escalate into a medical crisis. When the body’s immune system overreacts to the plant’s oils, or when the rash appears in sensitive areas, home remedies like oatmeal baths simply aren't enough. Knowing when to seek severe poison ivy treatment can mean the difference between a controlled recovery and a dangerous systemic reaction.

Understanding the "Itch"

The culprit behind your discomfort is an oil called urushiol. This sticky, colorless oil is found in the roots, stems, and leaves of poison ivy, oak, and sumac. According to NIEHS, about 85% of the population will have some reaction to urushiol during their lifetime. It only takes a microscopic amount to trigger an itchy, blistering eruption. The rash is a form of allergic contact dermatitis. While the initial contact doesn’t hurt, the reaction usually appears within 12 to 72 hours. While most cases stay localized, certain symptoms signal that the reaction is spreading or becoming severe.

Signs Your Rash Needs Urgent Care

Most people can manage a small patch of poison ivy with over-the-counter hydrocortisone. However, you should visit an urgent care center if:
  • The rash covers more than 25% of your body.
  • The itching is so intense that it prevents you from sleeping or performing daily tasks.
  • The blisters are oozing large amounts of fluid or pus, which could indicate a secondary bacterial infection.

Rashes on the Face or Eyes

One of the most critical reasons to seek severe poison ivy treatment is the location of the outbreak. Rashes on the face or eyes are particularly concerning. Because the skin around the eyes is incredibly thin and sensitive, swelling can occur rapidly. If your eyelids begin to swell, it can obstruct your vision or lead to an infection of the eye itself. The FDA warns that any involvement of the eyes, mouth, or genitals should be evaluated by a healthcare professional immediately to prevent complications.

Difficulty Breathing After Exposure

While skin contact is the most common way to react, the most dangerous exposure comes from fire. If poison ivy or oak is burned, the urushiol oil hitches a ride on smoke particles. Inhaling these particles can cause severe inflammation in the lungs. If you experience difficulty breathing after exposure to brush fire smoke or if you feel a "tightness" in your chest, this is a life-threatening emergency. You should call 911 or head to the nearest ER immediately. This can lead to severe respiratory distress that requires oxygen and intensive medical intervention.

When to Head Straight to the Emergency Room

Sometimes, a rash isn't just a skin issue; it’s a whole-body (systemic) event. You should seek emergency department care if you experience any of the following:
  1. Anaphylaxis: This is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction. Signs include hives, swelling of the tongue or throat, dizziness, and a rapid pulse.
  2. High Fever: If a fever over 100°F accompanies your rash, it may indicate that the skin is infected (cellulitis) or that the allergic response is severe.
  3. Widespread Blistering: If blisters are forming over large areas of the body or are appearing in the mouth.
  4. Difficulty Swallowing: This suggests that the swelling is affecting your airway or esophagus.

Prescription-Strength Relief

If you seek medical help, your provider has tools that go far beyond what you can buy at a drugstore. For those requiring severe poison ivy treatment, doctors often prescribe prescription-strength relief to calm the immune system.
  • Oral Corticosteroids: Medications like prednisone can reduce swelling and itching from the inside out. These are typically used for 10–14 days to prevent a "rebound" rash.
  • High-Potency Topical Steroids: Stronger than over-the-counter creams, these help flatten blisters and stop the itch on contact.
  • Antibiotics: If a secondary infection has set in from scratching, your doctor may prescribe a course of antibiotics to clear the skin.
As noted by the NIH, early intervention with steroids can significantly shorten the duration of the symptoms and prevent scarring.

Preventing the Spread

You cannot "catch" poison ivy from someone else’s blisters. The fluid inside the blisters does not contain urushiol. However, you can get it from touching the oil on unwashed clothing, gardening tools, or even a pet's fur. To prevent future outbreaks:
  • Wash everything: If you suspect exposure, wash your skin with soap and cool water immediately. Urushiol can bond to the skin within 10 to 20 minutes.
  • Clean tools: Use rubbing alcohol or soap to wipe down anything that might have touched the plants.
  • Identify the plants: Remember the mantra, "Leaves of three, let them be." Poison ivy and oak usually have three leaflets per stem.

Trust Your Instincts

You know your body better than anyone else. If a rash feels "different" than usual, or if the pain and swelling are making you anxious, don't wait. It is always better to have a medical professional tell you it's a standard case than to let a systemic reaction go untreated.

Is Your Poison Ivy Rash a Medical Crisis?

content.raw:
If you have recently returned from a long-haul flight or are recovering from a surgical procedure, your body has been through a lot. While you’re likely focused on getting back to your routine, it’s important to pay attention to how your legs feel. A blood clot in the deep veins, known as Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), is a serious condition that can develop when blood flow slows down or changes. According to the CDC, every year, as many as 900,000 Americans are affected by blood clots. The good news is that DVT is preventable and highly treatable when caught early. This guide will help you identify DVT symptoms, understand your risks, and know exactly when to reach out for professional medical help.

What is Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)?

Deep Vein Thrombosis occurs when a blood clot (thrombus) forms in one or more of the deep veins in your body, usually in your legs. Unlike the veins you can see just under your skin, deep veins are surrounded by muscle. When a clot forms here, it can block blood flow, causing pain and swelling.

Why Travel and Surgery Increase Your Risk

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), long-distance travel (more than four hours) increases your risk because you are sitting in a confined space for a long period. This inactivity causes blood to pool in your lower legs. Similarly, surgery is a major risk factor. Surgery can trigger the body’s natural clotting mechanism while also requiring periods of bed rest. Combined, these factors create a "perfect storm" for DVT to develop.

Recognizing DVT Symptoms: More Than Just a Cramp

DVT can be tricky because it doesn’t always cause obvious pain. CDC states that, in fact, about half of the people with DVT have no symptoms at all. However, when symptoms do appear, they typically affect only one leg.

Leg Swelling and Redness

One of the most common DVT symptoms is swelling in one leg. You might notice that your calf or thigh looks significantly larger than the other. This isn't the general puffiness you might get in both ankles after a long day; it is usually localized to the limb where the clot is located. Along with swelling, the skin may appear reddish or even bluish in color.

Tenderness and Warmth

If you touch the area that is swollen, it may feel warm to the touch compared to the surrounding skin. Many patients describe the pain as a "charley horse" or a severe cramp that just won’t go away. This tenderness often starts in the calf and can feel like soreness or a persistent ache when standing or walking.

The Risk of Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

According to MedlinePlus The most serious complication of DVT occurs if a piece of the blood clot breaks off and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs. This is called a Pulmonary Embolism (PE).

When a Blood Clot Travels to the Lungs

A PE is a life-threatening medical emergency. It blocks the blood flow to the lungs, which can damage the lung tissue and lower oxygen levels in your blood. It is important to remember that sometimes, the first sign of a DVT is actually the symptoms of a PE.

Warning Signs of a Medical Emergency

You should seek emergency medical care immediately if you experience:
  • Sudden shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.
  • Chest pain that worsens when you take a deep breath or cough.
  • A rapid or irregular heartbeat.
  • Feeling lightheaded, dizzy, or fainting.
  • Coughing up blood.

Who is Most at Risk for DVT?

While anyone can develop a clot, certain factors make it more likely. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) identifies several risk factors:
  • Age: Being over age 60, though DVT can occur at any age.
  • Recent Injury or Surgery: Especially surgeries involving the hips, knees, or abdomen.
  • Immobility: Being on bed rest or sitting for long periods.
  • Pregnancy: The increased pressure in the veins of the pelvis and legs.
  • Health Conditions: Including cancer, heart disease, or inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Medications: Such as birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy.

How We Diagnose DVT: On-site Blood Tests and Imaging

If you visit an urgent care or emergency room with suspected DVT symptoms, healthcare providers use specific tools to find the clot quickly.
  1. D-dimer Test: This is a specialized blood test that measures a substance in the blood that is released when a blood clot breaks up. If the test is negative, it likely means you do not have a clot.
  2. Duplex Ultrasound: This is the most common test for DVT. It uses sound waves to create images of the blood flow in your veins. It is non-invasive, painless, and can usually be done right in the clinic.
  3. Venography: In rarer cases, if an ultrasound doesn't provide a clear answer, a provider might use a venogram, where dye is injected into a vein to make it visible on an X-ray.
It regulates the medications and diagnostic tools used to manage these conditions, ensuring they meet high safety standards for patient care.

Immediate Steps to Take if You Suspect a Clot

If you notice swelling, redness, or unexplained pain in one leg after a trip or surgery, do not wait. Do not massage the leg, as this could potentially dislodge a clot and cause it to travel to your lungs. Instead, keep the leg elevated and contact a healthcare professional immediately. Early diagnosis often means treatment can begin with blood thinners (anticoagulants), which prevent the clot from getting larger while your body slowly reabsorbs it.

When to Get Checked for a Blood Clot

If you’ve recently traveled or had surgery and have unexplained pain, swelling, or warmth in one leg, do not wait. A clot can travel to the lungs within hours, so get evaluated for a blood clot at ER of Irving right away. We are open 24/7. Need immediate care? Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

How long after surgery can a DVT occur?

The risk is highest in the first few days to weeks after surgery, but the NIH suggests that the risk can remain elevated for up to three months post-operation.

Can DVT happen in both legs at the same time?

While it is possible, it is very rare. DVT typically presents in only one leg. If both legs are equally swollen, it may be due to another condition like heart failure or general fluid retention.

Does walking help DVT?

Walking is a great way to prevent DVT by keeping blood flowing. However, if you already suspect you have a clot, you should consult a doctor before engaging in heavy exercise to ensure the clot is stable.

Will a DVT go away on its own?

Your body can eventually break down a clot, but without medical treatment, the risk of the clot growing or moving to the lungs is dangerously high. Medical intervention is always necessary.

What does DVT pain feel like?

It often feels like a persistent, throbbing cramp or soreness, usually in the calf. It may feel worse when you flex your foot upward.

Can I fly if I have DVT?

You should not fly with an untreated DVT. Once you are on stable treatment (like blood thinners) and cleared by your doctor, travel may be possible.

We’ve all been there: a slip of the kitchen knife, a tumble on the pavement, or a DIY project gone wrong. In those first few seconds after a deep cut, your mind starts racing. Is it deep? Does it need a doctor? Should I just use a bandage and hope for the best? Deciding whether you need Professional medical attention for a wound is more than just about stopping the bleeding. It’s about preventing infection, ensuring the wound heals with minimal scarring, and making sure no underlying nerves or tendons are damaged. If you are searching for stitches in Irving, TX, you likely need a quick, clear answer so you can take action. This guide will walk you through how to assess a laceration, what the treatment options look like, and how to stay safe on your way to the ER.

How to Tell if Your Cut Needs Professional Care

Not every scrape requires a trip to the emergency room or urgent care, but deep lacerations are different. According to MedlinePlus, a wound generally needs professional closure if it meets certain criteria.

The Depth and Length Rule

If a cut is deeper than a quarter-inch, you can see "yellow fat," or if the wound is gaping so wide that you cannot easily pull the edges together with gentle pressure, you likely need stitches. Any wound longer than half an inch often requires medical intervention to heal properly.

Persistent Bleeding

If you apply direct pressure to a wound for 10 to 15 minutes and it is still bleeding actively, this is a medical emergency. High-pressure "spurting" blood indicates an arterial injury, which requires immediate care at an ER.

Location Matters

The location of the cut significantly changes the treatment plan.
  • The Face: Cuts on the face are often treated with extra care to minimize scarring.
  • Joints: Lacerations over knuckles, elbows, or knees are difficult to keep closed with simple bandages because the skin stretches every time you move.
  • Hands and Feet: ASSH states that because we use our hands for almost everything, deep cuts here carry a higher risk of nerve or tendon damage.

Stitches vs. Medical Glue: What’s the Difference?

When you arrive at the ER for stitches in Irving, TX, the provider will evaluate whether "traditional" sutures or modern medical adhesives are best for your specific injury.

When Doctors Choose Traditional Sutures (Stitches)

Stitches (sutures) are the "gold standard" for deep or complex wounds. They are made of sterile thread-like material that manually holds the skin edges together.
  • Best for: Deep cuts, wounds over joints, or jagged lacerations.
  • Pros: They are incredibly strong and can hold high-tension areas together while they heal.
  • Cons: They require a follow-up visit for removal (unless they are the "absorbable" kind) and can be slightly more intimidating for children.

The Benefits of Medical Adhesive (Skin Glue)

Medical glue, often called "dermabond," is a specialized liquid adhesive. According to the FDA, these adhesives are designed to slough off naturally as the wound heals.
  • Best for: Small, straight cuts in areas with low tension (like the forehead or shins).
  • Pros: No needles are required, the process is very fast, and there is no need for a return visit to have them removed.
  • Cons: Glue cannot be used on joints, hairy areas, or wounds that are heavily bleeding or contaminated.

How long can you wait to get stitches?

Timing is everything when it comes to wound care. You should generally seek medical attention within 6 to 12 hours of the injury. Waiting too long increases the risk of infection significantly. Once a wound has been open for several hours, bacteria begin to colonize the area. If you wait more than 24 hours, many doctors will refuse to "stitch the wound shut" because doing so could trap bacteria inside, leading to a serious abscess or systemic infection. Early closure leads to better cosmetic results and faster return to normal activity. If you are unsure, it is always better to be evaluated sooner rather than later.

Caring for the wound on the way to the ER or Urgent Care

The steps you take in the first 20 minutes after an injury can make a huge difference in your recovery. Here is how to handle a deep laceration while you are en route to get stitches, Irving, TX:
  1. Apply Direct Pressure: Use a clean cloth or sterile gauze. Hold firm, steady pressure directly over the site for at least 10 minutes without "peeking" to see if it stopped.
  2. Elevate: If the injury is on an arm or leg, keep it raised above the level of your heart to slow the blood flow.
  3. Clean Gently (If Possible): If there is visible dirt, you can rinse the wound with cool water. NIH recommends not scrubbing the wound or using harsh chemicals like hydrogen peroxide or iodine, as these can actually damage the healthy tissue and slow down healing.
  4. Cover: Once bleeding is controlled, wrap the area in a clean bandage. Do not apply antibiotic ointments until a doctor has seen the wound, as it can interfere with medical glue if that ends up being the chosen treatment.

Tetanus shot updates: Why they matter for deep cuts

Whenever the skin is broken, especially by a dirty object, metal, or an animal bite, doctors worry about tetanus. Tetanus is a serious disease caused by bacteria found in soil, dust, and manure that enter the body through breaks in the skin. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get a tetanus booster (Td or Tdap) every 10 years. However, for a "dirty" or deep wound, a doctor may recommend a booster if your last shot was more than 5 years ago. Staying up to date on your vaccines is one of the simplest ways to prevent a life-threatening complication from a simple accident.

What to Expect During Your Visit

When you visit an urgent care or ER for a laceration, the process is usually straightforward:
  • Numbing: For stitches, the doctor will likely use a local anesthetic (like Lidocaine) to numb the area so you don’t feel a thing.
  • Irrigation: The wound will be thoroughly washed with sterile saline to remove any hidden debris.
  • Closure: The provider will use sutures, staples, or glue to close the skin.
  • Aftercare Instructions: You’ll receive specific instructions on how to keep the wound dry and when to return for a check-up.

Need Immediate Care for a Deep Cut in Irving, TX?

When accidents happen, waiting isn't an option. Whether you are dealing with persistent bleeding, a wound over a joint, or you are unsure whether you need stitches or medical glue, the ER of Irving is here to help. A deep cut closed within 6 to 12 hours has a lower risk of infection and scarring, and any wound that spurts blood or will not stop bleeding after 10 to 15 minutes of pressure needs emergency care now. See the emergency services at ER of Irving. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (972) 893-3148 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Does it hurt to get stitches?

The injury itself is usually the most painful part. Before placing stitches, providers use a very small needle to numb the area.

Can I use super glue from the store on a cut?

No. Household super glue contains chemicals that can irritate skin tissue and cause chemical burns. Medical-grade glue is sterile and specifically formulated to be flexible and safe for human tissue.

How do I know if my cut is infected?

Signs of infection include increasing pain, swelling, warmth around the wound, red streaks leading away from the cut, or pus-like drainage. If you have a fever, seek medical help immediately.

How long do stitches stay in?

It depends on the location. Stitches on the face may come out in 3–5 days to prevent scarring, while stitches on the joints or feet may need to stay in for 10–14 days.

Can I get my stitches wet?

Usually, you must keep the area dry for the first 24 to 48 hours. After that, your doctor may allow gentle washing with soap and water, but you should avoid soaking in a tub or pool until the stitches are removed.

Will I have a scar?

All deep cuts result in some level of scarring, but getting professional closure (stitches or glue) significantly reduces the size and visibility of the scar compared to letting the wound heal "open."

If you are searching for stitches in Irving, TX, you likely need a quick, clear answer so you can take action.

This guide will walk you through how to assess a laceration, what the treatment options look like, and how to stay safe on your way to the ER.

How to Tell if Your Cut Needs Professional Care

Not every scrape requires a trip to the emergency room or urgent care, but deep lacerations are different. According to MedlinePlus, a wound generally needs professional closure if it meets certain criteria.

The Depth and Length Rule

If a cut is deeper than a quarter-inch, you can see “yellow fat,” or if the wound is gaping so wide that you cannot easily pull the edges together with gentle pressure, you likely need stitches. Any wound longer than half an inch often requires medical intervention to heal properly.

Persistent Bleeding

If you apply direct pressure to a wound for 10 to 15 minutes and it is still bleeding actively, this is a medical emergency. High-pressure “spurting” blood indicates an arterial injury, which requires immediate care at an ER.

Location Matters

The location of the cut significantly changes the treatment plan.

  • The Face: Cuts on the face are often treated with extra care to minimize scarring.
  • Joints: Lacerations over knuckles, elbows, or knees are difficult to keep closed with simple bandages because the skin stretches every time you move.
  • Hands and Feet: ASSH states that because we use our hands for almost everything, deep cuts here carry a higher risk of nerve or tendon damage.

Stitches vs. Medical Glue: What’s the Difference?

When you arrive at the ER for stitches in Irving, TX, the provider will evaluate whether “traditional” sutures or modern medical adhesives are best for your specific injury.

When Doctors Choose Traditional Sutures (Stitches)

Stitches (sutures) are the “gold standard” for deep or complex wounds. They are made of sterile thread-like material that manually holds the skin edges together.

  • Best for: Deep cuts, wounds over joints, or jagged lacerations.
  • Pros: They are incredibly strong and can hold high-tension areas together while they heal.
  • Cons: They require a follow-up visit for removal (unless they are the “absorbable” kind) and can be slightly more intimidating for children.

The Benefits of Medical Adhesive (Skin Glue)

Medical glue, often called “dermabond,” is a specialized liquid adhesive. According to the FDA, these adhesives are designed to slough off naturally as the wound heals.

  • Best for: Small, straight cuts in areas with low tension (like the forehead or shins).
  • Pros: No needles are required, the process is very fast, and there is no need for a return visit to have them removed.
  • Cons: Glue cannot be used on joints, hairy areas, or wounds that are heavily bleeding or contaminated.

How long can you wait to get stitches?

Timing is everything when it comes to wound care. You should generally seek medical attention within 6 to 12 hours of the injury.

Waiting too long increases the risk of infection significantly. Once a wound has been open for several hours, bacteria begin to colonize the area. If you wait more than 24 hours, many doctors will refuse to “stitch the wound shut” because doing so could trap bacteria inside, leading to a serious abscess or systemic infection.

Early closure leads to better cosmetic results and faster return to normal activity. If you are unsure, it is always better to be evaluated sooner rather than later.

Caring for the wound on the way to the ER or Urgent Care

The steps you take in the first 20 minutes after an injury can make a huge difference in your recovery. Here is how to handle a deep laceration while you are en route to get stitches, Irving, TX:

  1. Apply Direct Pressure: Use a clean cloth or sterile gauze. Hold firm, steady pressure directly over the site for at least 10 minutes without “peeking” to see if it stopped.
  2. Elevate: If the injury is on an arm or leg, keep it raised above the level of your heart to slow the blood flow.
  3. Clean Gently (If Possible): If there is visible dirt, you can rinse the wound with cool water. NIH recommends not scrubbing the wound or using harsh chemicals like hydrogen peroxide or iodine, as these can actually damage the healthy tissue and slow down healing.
  4. Cover: Once bleeding is controlled, wrap the area in a clean bandage. Do not apply antibiotic ointments until a doctor has seen the wound, as it can interfere with medical glue if that ends up being the chosen treatment.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get a tetanus booster (Td or Tdap) every 10 years. However, for a “dirty” or deep wound, a doctor may recommend a booster if your last shot was more than 5 years ago. Staying up to date on your vaccines is one of the simplest ways to prevent a life-threatening complication from a simple accident.

When you visit an urgent care or ER for a laceration, the process is usually straightforward:

  • Numbing: For stitches, the doctor will likely use a local anesthetic (like Lidocaine) to numb the area so you don’t feel a thing.
  • Irrigation: The wound will be thoroughly washed with sterile saline to remove any hidden debris.
  • Closure: The provider will use sutures, staples, or glue to close the skin.
  • Aftercare Instructions: You’ll receive specific instructions on how to keep the wound dry and when to return for a check-up.

Whether you are dealing with persistent bleeding, a wound over a joint, or you are unsure whether you need stitches or medical glue, the ER of Irving is here to help. The injury itself is usually the most painful part. Before placing stitches, providers use a very small needle to numb the area.

Can I use super glue from the store on a cut?

No. Household super glue contains chemicals that can irritate skin tissue and cause chemical burns. Medical-grade glue is sterile and specifically formulated to be flexible and safe for human tissue.

title.rendered: Difficulty Swallowing: Is it a Peritonsillar Abscess?

content.raw:
We have all been there, that scratchy, uncomfortable feeling in the back of the throat that makes it hard to enjoy a meal. Usually, it’s a cold or perhaps a routine case of strep throat that clears up with rest. But sometimes, a sore throat isn't just a nuisance; it becomes a serious medical situation. When the pain becomes so intense that you can’t swallow your own saliva or your voice sounds different to your family, it’s natural to feel anxious. You might be dealing with a peritonsillar abscess, a condition that requires prompt medical evaluation. Understanding the difference between a typical infection and an emergency can help you get the care you need before things get worse.

What is a Peritonsillar Abscess?

MedlinePlus states that a peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus that forms in the tissues of the throat next to one of the tonsils. It often starts as a complication of tonsillitis or strep throat. When the infection breaks through the tonsil and spreads into the surrounding area, the body tries to wall it off, creating a painful, swollen pocket. While this condition (historically called "quinsy") is most common in adolescents and young adults, it can happen to anyone. According to NIH, because the abscess can grow large enough to shift the structures of your throat, it is considered a serious infection that warrants a severe sore throat ER visit if it begins to interfere with your breathing.

When Strep Throat Gets Dangerous

Most cases of strep throat resolve beautifully with a standard course of antibiotics. However, if the bacteria, usually Streptococcus pyogenes, are particularly aggressive or if treatment is delayed, the infection can invade deeper tissues.

The Progression of Infection

When strep throat gets dangerous, the infection moves beyond the surface of the tonsils. It can lead to cellulitis (skin/tissue infection) and eventually the formation of an abscess. This is why medical professionals emphasize finishing your entire antibiotic prescription, even if you feel better after two days. Stopping early can allow lingering bacteria to migrate and cause deeper, more complex pockets of infection.

Recognizing the Red Flags: Symptoms You Can’t Ignore

How do you know if your sore throat has crossed the line into an emergency? A peritonsillar abscess usually presents with symptoms that are much more "one-sided" and severe than a typical viral cold.

Trouble Opening the Mouth

NIH states that one of the most telling signs of an abscess is trismus, or trouble opening the mouth. Because the infection is so close to the muscles used for chewing, the inflammation causes those muscles to spasm. If you find you can only open your mouth a crack to take a sip of water, this is a major red flag.

The "Hot Potato" Voice

Doctors often look for a symptom called the "hot potato voice." This is a muffled quality to your speech, sounding as if you are trying to talk with a mouthful of hot food. MedlinePlus states that this happens because the swelling is physically obstructing the throat and affecting the movement of the soft palate.

Other Warning Signs:

  • Drooling: If it hurts too much to swallow your own spit, it will begin to pool in your mouth.
  • Swollen Lymph Nodes: You may feel a very large, tender lump under your jaw on the affected side.
  • Uvular Deviation: If you look in a mirror and see the "dangly bit" (uvula) at the back of your throat pushed to one side, the abscess is likely pushing against it.

Is it just a Sore Throat or an Emergency?

It can be difficult for a patient to self-diagnose, but comparing these symptoms can help you decide where to go for care.
Symptom Viral Sore Throat Strep Throat Peritonsillar Abscess
Pain Level Mild to Moderate Severe Excruciating
Fever Sometimes Usually Often High
Swelling Symmetrical Symmetrical One-Sided (Asymmetric)
Ability to Swallow Uncomfortable Difficult Nearly Impossible
Voice Quality Raspy/Hoarse Normal Muffled/Hot Potato
If you are experiencing the symptoms in the far-right column, you should seek an ER evaluation for a severe sore throat. A primary care doctor may not have the specialized tools needed to treat an advanced abscess in the office.

Diagnosis and Immediate Care

When you arrive at an urgent care or emergency room, the medical team will likely perform a physical exam and perhaps an intraoral ultrasound or CT scan to see the exact size and location of the pocket.

Emergency Drainage and Antibiotics

The primary treatment for a peritonsillar abscess involves two steps: emergency drainage and antibiotics.
  1. Drainage (Aspiration): NIH recommends that to provide immediate relief and stop the spread of infection, a doctor will often need to drain the pus. This is typically done by numbing the area and using a needle to withdraw the fluid or by making a small incision. While it sounds intimidating, most patients feel an immense, immediate reduction in pain once the pressure is released.
  2. Antibiotics: Once the abscess is drained, you will be started on high-dose antibiotics, sometimes delivered intravenously (IV) initially to ensure they get into your system quickly.
  3. Steroids: In many cases, doctors will also prescribe steroids to reduce the intense swelling, making it easier for you to breathe and swallow.

Prevention and Long-Term Recovery

The best way to prevent an abscess is to treat throat infections early. If you are diagnosed with strep, follow the treatment plan exactly. According to NIH, if you suffer from chronic tonsillitis (frequent infections), your doctor might eventually recommend a tonsillectomy, the surgical removal of the tonsils to prevent future abscesses from forming. During recovery, focus on hydration. Even if it is difficult, small sips of cool liquids are vital. Most people recover fully within a week or two after proper drainage and antibiotic therapy.
